questions.q: How did Paul Dirac come to predict the existence of antimatter?
options: He observed an unexplained track in a cloud chamber and named the particle responsible
His relativistic equation for the electron had negative-energy solutions that he eventually interpreted as a new particle with the electron's mass and opposite charge
He measured the charge of the electron and found a positive value he could not explain
He fired cosmic rays at a lead plate and detected positive particles
questions.explanation: Dirac predicted antimatter purely from the internal logic of his equation, not from any experiment. The second set of (negative-energy) solutions led him, by 1931, to declare a new 'anti-electron' with the same mass as the electron but opposite charge.

questions.q: How did Carl Anderson identify the positron in his cloud chamber in 1932?
options: It left a much heavier, denser track than an electron
It had the mass of an electron but curved the opposite way in the magnetic field, showing a positive charge
It travelled faster than light and left no droplet trail
It was repelled by the lead plate placed across the chamber
questions.explanation: The track was as faint and wispy as an electron's (same tiny mass) but curved the opposite way in the magnetic field, marking a positive charge. The 6 mm lead plate let Anderson confirm the direction of travel, proving it was Dirac's anti-electron.

questions.q: When a positron and an electron annihilate, why are exactly two gamma rays produced, flying off in opposite directions?
options: The two particles are both negatively charged and repel into two beams
Conservation of momentum: the pair is nearly at rest with near-zero total momentum, so the photons must fly back-to-back with equal and opposite momenta that cancel
Conservation of charge requires two photons to carry away the charge
The gamma rays are emitted from the two separate nuclei involved
questions.explanation: Because the annihilating pair is essentially at rest, total momentum is near zero. A single photon always carries momentum, so two photons are needed, fired at 180 degrees so their momenta cancel and the total stays zero.

questions.q: By what process does fluorine-18 produce a positron inside the patient, and which force drives it?
options: Alpha decay, driven by the strong nuclear force
Beta-plus decay, in which a proton becomes a neutron and emits a positron and a neutrino, driven by the weak nuclear force
Gamma decay, driven by the electromagnetic force
Beta-minus decay, in which a neutron becomes a proton, driven by the weak nuclear force
questions.explanation: Fluorine-18 has too many protons, so it undergoes beta-plus decay: a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino. Only the weak nuclear force can change one kind of particle into another like this, turning F-18 into O-18.

questions.q: Why does the radioactive sugar FDG accumulate most in cancer cells?
options: Cancer cells are magnetic and attract the fluorine atom
Cancer cells consume glucose at a furious rate (the Warburg effect), and the modified FDG gets phosphate-tagged and trapped inside them
FDG is repelled by healthy tissue and only dissolves in tumours
Cancer cells convert FDG directly into gamma rays
questions.explanation: Cancer cells are gluttons for glucose (the Warburg effect), so they take up the glucose-mimic FDG fastest. Because of the swapped fluorine atom, FDG is tagged with phosphate and then gets stuck, accumulating in the hungriest cells.

questions.q: What does the PET scanner actually detect, and how does it locate where an annihilation occurred?
options: It detects the positrons directly as they leave the body
It detects pairs of 511 keV gamma rays arriving at opposite detectors at almost the same instant (a coincidence), placing the annihilation on the line of response between them
It detects the neutrinos emitted during beta-plus decay
It detects the heat released by trapped FDG molecules
questions.explanation: The positrons never leave the body; they annihilate within a millimetre or two. The scanner catches the two back-to-back gamma rays, and a coincidence between opposite detectors defines a line of response. Where millions of lines cross is where the sugar is concentrated.

questions.q: Why is fluorine-18's half-life of about 110 minutes described as a 'Goldilocks' compromise?
options: It is long enough to make the gamma rays more energetic, but short enough to avoid overheating the patient
It is long enough to ship the tracer and let the sugar be taken up before scanning, yet short enough that the patient clears the radioactivity by the next day
It exactly matches the time it takes a positron to find an electron
It is the half-life that produces the most positrons per second
questions.explanation: Carbon-11's 20-minute half-life is too short to ship; a very long half-life would leave the patient radioactive for days. F-18's ~110 minutes is long enough to manufacture, ship, inject and wait for uptake, but short enough to essentially clear within a day (about six half-lives in ~11 hours).

questions.q: From memory: state the three conservation laws satisfied in positron-electron annihilation, and what each one fixes.
keyPoints: Conservation of mass-energy (E = mc^2): the particles' rest mass converts entirely to photon energy, fixing each photon at 511 keV.
Conservation of momentum: the pair is near rest with zero total momentum, so two photons fly out back-to-back (180 degrees) and their momenta cancel.
Conservation of charge: electron (-1) plus positron (+1) gives zero, and the two outgoing photons are neutral, so charge is zero before and after.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three laws and tied energy to the 511 keV photon energy and momentum to the 180-degree direction, grade Good or Easy. Missing charge conservation, or the link to direction/energy, grade Hard or Again.

questions.q: From memory: explain why the gamma rays a PET scanner detects are NOT emitted from the nucleus, and where the positrons end up.
keyPoints: The gamma rays are born outside the nucleus, from the annihilation of a positron with an electron in the surrounding tissue.
This is different from ordinary gamma decay, where the photon comes from the nucleus itself.
The positrons never leave the body; they annihilate within about a millimetre or two of where they were created, so only their gamma-ray light escapes.
questions.explanation: If you distinguished annihilation photons (outside the nucleus) from nuclear gamma decay, and noted that the positrons die inside the tissue, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: An electron and a positron, each with a rest mass energy of 511 keV, annihilate from rest. Find the total energy released and the energy of each of the two gamma rays produced.
questions.given: Rest mass energy of electron = rest mass energy of positron = 511 keV; the pair annihilates from rest into two equal photons.
working: Total energy released = sum of the two rest mass energies (E = mc^2 for each):
By symmetry the two photons share this energy equally:
questions.explanation: Each particle contributes its 511 keV rest mass energy, giving 1.022 MeV total. Momentum conservation forces two equal back-to-back photons, so each carries exactly 511 keV.

questions.q: Explain why the two gamma rays from positron-electron annihilation are emitted almost, but not exactly, 180 degrees apart. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Conservation of momentum requires that the total momentum after annihilation equals the total before. If the electron and positron were perfectly at rest, their total momentum would be exactly zero, forcing the two photons to fly out at exactly 180 degrees so their momenta cancel. In reality the pair retains a tiny residual momentum at the moment of annihilation, so the total momentum is not perfectly zero, and the photons emerge a fraction of a degree off a perfect straight line. This non-collinearity is a fundamental limit on PET image sharpness: the conservation law is exact, but the starting momentum is not perfectly zero.

criteria.descriptor: States that conservation of momentum forces the photons back-to-back when the pair is at rest.
Identifies that the real pair has a small residual (non-zero) momentum at annihilation.
Concludes the photons are slightly off 180 degrees (non-collinearity), limiting image sharpness.

questions.explanation: The marker rewards linking the (exact) momentum conservation law to the (imperfect) near-zero starting momentum of the real pair.
